name: Cable Chest Press

claims.text: Set the two pulleys at chest height and stand a foot or two in front of them, one handle in each hand.

quotes.text: Position the dual pulleys of a functional trainer to chest height and select an appropriate weight.
Stand a foot or two in front of the cables, holding one d-handle in each hand.
Set cable pulleys at chest height on a crossover machine.

claims.text: Stand with one foot in front of the other (a staggered stance) for stability, feet planted.

quotes.text: Place one foot in front of the other.
Keep the feet planted on the floor.
You can stagger your stance for better stability.

claims.text: Handles just outside shoulder width; a neutral (hammer) grip is suggested so the shoulder moves freely; elbows just below 90 degrees, wrists lined up with the elbows; press straight ahead, pushing through the palms.

quotes.text: Stand in front of the cable machine with the handles just outside shoulder width. We suggest a neutral (hammer) grip as this allows the shoulder to move more freely. Keep your arms just below 90 degrees and press straight ahead.
Keep the elbows just below 90 degrees and make sure the wrist and elbows line up.
Push through the palms of the hand.

claims.text: Bring the handles back to about nipple height: below that is too low, near the collarbone is too high.

quotes.text: Bring the cable handles to roughly where your nipples are. Below the nipples is too low and going near the collar bone is too high.

claims.text: Let the handles come back toward the chest over 2-3 seconds, stopping about an inch short of it; press out briskly without fully locking the elbows.

quotes.text: Lower the cables towards the chest to about one inch before touching the chest. Do this in a controlled 2-3 second tempo.
Push the cables back to the starting position in a semi explosive tempo. Do not completely lock the elbow just extend it so it is almost locked.

claims.text: Keep a neutral spine and brace the abdominals, glutes and legs; do not arch the back, which can cause lower-back pain.

quotes.text: Keep a neutral spine; brace abdominals, glutes, and lower body.
Arching your back: This can cause lower back pain and remove the core stability challenge. Keep your spine neutral and brace your abs during the exercise.

claims.text: Named common mistakes: shrugging the shoulders, shifting and jerking the body, gripping much wider than shoulder width, flaring the elbows and using too much weight.

quotes.text: Shrugging the shoulders.
Shifting and jerking your body.
Do not grip much wider than shoulder width, it will put stress on the shoulder.

Flaring your elbows: This can put excessive stress on your shoulder joints and reduce the activation of your chest muscles. Keep your elbows at a 45-degree angle from your body throughout the movement.
Using too much weight: This can compromise your form and increase the risk of injury.

claims.text: Do not let ego pick the weight, because form suffers.

quotes.text: Do not let your ego dictate the weight you use because your form will suffer.

claims.text: Muscles: chest is the main mover; front shoulder and triceps help.

quotes.text: Primary muscles worked: Chest Secondary muscles worked: Front Deltoid Triceps

claims.text: Pressing from standing is limited mainly by whole-body stability and trunk coordination rather than maximal chest and shoulder activation: in recreationally trained men the one-arm standing cable press 1RM was far below the bench press 1RM, and trunk muscles worked hard.

quotes.text: The 1RM BP performance resulted in an average load (74.2 +/- 17.6 kg) significantly higher than 1RM single-arm SP (26.0 +/- 4.4 kg).
Our EMG findings show that SCP performance is limited by the activation and neuromuscular coordination of torso muscles, not maximal muscle activation of the chest and shoulder muscles.

The SCP performance also relies on the strength of shoulder and chest musculature; however, it is whole-body stability and equilibrium together with joint stability that present the major limitation in force generation.

claims.text: Chest and front-shoulder activity is higher in more stable pushing; less stable pushing raises abdominal and trunk work.

quotes.text: Pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, and anterior serratus are highly elicited during more stable pushing conditions, whereas abdominal muscles, triceps brachii, posterior deltoid, and upper trapezius are affected in the opposite manner.

claims.text: In a lab study, shoulder moments were larger in the cable pulley chest exercises than in the bench press (measured on the cable cross-over and pull-over, not a press; applied here by inference).

quotes.text: The maximum absolute moments at the shoulder joint were significantly larger for the cable pulley exercises than for the bench press exercises.
as well as during two different cable pulley exercises, namely the cross-over exercise, also known as butterfly, and the pull-over exercise at moderate intensity.

claims.text: Up to 36% of documented resistance-training injuries are at the shoulder, and poor attention to technique is a named risk factor.

quotes.text: The results of the review indicated that up to 36% of documented RT-related injuries and disorders occur at the shoulder complex.
extrinsic risk factors, namely, that of improper attention to exercise technique

claims.text: Add load in small steps: ACSM recommends a 2-10% increase once the current load can be done for one to two reps over the target.

quotes.text: it is recommended that 2-10% increase in load be applied when the individual can perform the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number

claims.text: Tempo: lower in a controlled 2-3 seconds; the press back is only 'semi explosive', so the 1 s up is a drawing convention (no source gives its seconds).

quotes.text: Lower the cables towards the chest to about one inch before touching the chest. Do this in a controlled 2-3 second tempo.
Push the cables back to the starting position in a semi explosive tempo. Do not completely lock the elbow just extend it so it is almost locked.

claims.text: Tempo: Motra lists a 2-1-2 tempo for this lift without saying which phase each digit is; read either way it gives 2 s down and 2 s up, and read as lower, pause, press, a 1 s pause at the bottom.

plate.viewWhy: Census view is side; the staggered stance, the handle height at the nipples and the back position read in the sagittal plane (c2, c4, c6). One column shows in side view.
plate.equipment: Cable column with the pulley at chest height and a single handle (c1); the lifter stands a foot or two in front, staggered stance (c1, c2); floor line.
plate.start: Standing in a staggered stance, feet planted (c2), spine neutral and braced (c6); handles at about nipple height, elbows just below 90 degrees, wrists over the elbows (c3, c4).
plate.end: Arms pressed straight ahead to almost-straight elbows, not locked (c3, c5); body still (c7).

checkpoints.label: Staggered stance
checkpoints.what: One foot in front of the other, feet planted.

checkpoints.label: Handles at nipples
checkpoints.what: Handles come back to about nipple height, not the collarbone.

checkpoints.label: Spine neutral
checkpoints.what: Abs and glutes braced, back not arched.

mistake.what: Arching the lower back to push the handles out.
mistake.why: Bells of Steel names it among the most common cable chest press mistakes and links it to lower-back pain; NFPT asks for a neutral, braced spine. How often it happens is not measured.
mistake.rankNote: No source measures how often each fault happens. LR-31 step 2, tie left after step 3: STOPPED for a supervisor ruling. Step 1: no frequency word counts for a fault. Set aside: Bells of Steel's "Here are the most common mistakes to avoid on the cable chest press." is a list sentence; Schutz's "Injuries to the shoulder are very common in sports that involve overhead arm or throwing movements." is about other sports and "Another common method to improve chest muscle strength is to perform strength exercises on a cable pulley system" about the equipment (c12); Kolber's "the most prevalent regions of injury" (c13) names no fault. Step 2: four named faults are tied to harm, each on a common-mistakes list written for this exercise: flared elbows, "Flaring your elbows: This can put excessive stress on your shoulder joints and reduce the activation of your chest muscles." (Bells of Steel, c7); the arched back, "Arching your back: This can cause lower back pain and remove the core stability challenge." (Bells of Steel, c6; the head's pick); and the shoulder blades not pulled back, "Lack of retraction causes the scapula to anteriorly tilt and elevate the humerus. This can lead to an impingement of the subacromial bursa and the supraspinatus." (NFPT, the anchor; not on the card); and locked elbows, by Motra's cue "Keep slight elbow bend to protect joints." for its "Locking elbows at extension." (a cue that protects names harm, as on shoulder_press and landmine_row; NFPT's "Do not completely lock the elbow", c5, states none). Tie order: all four are on a list; one source ties each to harm; all are sourced directly; Bells of Steel's list names the elbows before the back, and Motra's names the locked elbows (second) before "Arching lower back." (fourth), so the back drops out; no list names two of the flared elbows, the retraction and the locked elbows. Step 3 then reads several ways: the first candidate on a list (the flared elbows open Bells of Steel's list after the load line; the locked elbows follow Motra's "Swinging or using momentum.", which is speed only), or the anchor's list, which names only the retraction. The census viewWhy names neither, so LR-36 cannot keep a pick. Set aside: NFPT's "Do not grip much wider than shoulder width, it will put stress on the shoulder." is a grip width (R-LB2-3); if grip width counts as a candidate it joins the tie on the anchor's list, before the retraction. Bells of Steel's "Using too much weight: This can compromise your form and increase the risk of injury." is the load. Until the ruling, plate.mistake (the arch) and handlingMistakes are unchanged.

tells.text: Body stays still as you press

tempo.text: Down 2 s sits inside NFPT's 2-3 s lowering (c15). NFPT gives no seconds for the press, only 'semi explosive', so the 1 s up is a drawing convention (c15, WEAK). Motra lists a 2-1-2 tempo (c16, WEAK: the page does not say which phase each digit is); read either way it gives 2 s up, so the up value is listed for a supervisor ruling (LR-33: sourced seconds are never replaced by the convention; R-LB2-1) and is not changed yet. Pause 0: no quote asks for a pause right after the press; Motra's "Squeeze chest at peak contraction." gives no pause or seconds. Read as lower, pause, press, Motra's middle 1 s is a bottom pause, so it is named here and not written in pause (LR-33, R-PB-3).

grip.type: Single handles; a neutral (hammer) grip is suggested (c3).
grip.width: Handles just outside shoulder width, not much wider (c3, c7).
grip.thumb: Not given by any cable press source read (push archetype default).
grip.wrist: Wrists lined up with the elbows (c3).

setup.step: Set both pulleys at chest height with single handles.
Stand a foot or two from the cables, a handle per hand.
Step into a staggered stance, feet planted.
Handles just outside shoulders, elbows just below 90 degrees, wrists over elbows.
Brace your abs and glutes, spine neutral.

posture.point: Spine neutral, abs and glutes braced.
Handles back to about nipple height.
Wrists in line with the elbows.
Elbows almost straight at the front, not locked.

handlingMistakes.fix: Keep your spine neutral and brace your abs.
Choose a weight you can press with the body still.
Handles just outside shoulder width, elbows about 45 degrees from the body.

rows.where: Chest, front shoulders, backs of arms

rows.means: Normal: standing presses load the trunk to keep you stable.

rows.fix: Stop and don't train through the pain. Keep your spine neutral.

rows.means: Fault: gripping much wider than shoulder width, or flaring the elbows.
rows.fix: Stop and don't train through the pain. Keep elbows at a 45-degree angle.

risks.risk: Wide grips and flared elbows stress the shoulder, a common injury site in lifting.
Too much weight costs form and raises injury risk. Add weight in small steps.

zooms.right: Neutral grip, wrist lined up with the elbow.
zooms.wrong: Wrist bent out of line with the elbow.

zooms.right: Staggered stance, spine neutral, handles at nipple height.
zooms.wrong: Lower back arched, handles up at the collarbone.
